core: What a food system is (production through disposal) and sustainability applied to food
Environmental footprint of food: land use, freshwater withdrawals, greenhouse-gas emissions share (with year and range)
Sustainable practices: regenerative agriculture, cover crops, reduced/no-till, crop rotation, IPM, agroforestry (USDA/NRCS)
Food loss and waste: scale in the U.S. and the national reduction goal
Diet and emissions: animal products vs plant foods per calorie/protein (Poore & Nemecek 2018)

Methane and nitrous oxide make agricultural emissions chemically distinct (pointer to Greenhouse Gases lesson)

claims.claim: Roughly half of the world's habitable land is used for agriculture, and about three-quarters of that farmland is used for livestock, which supplies only about 18% of global calories.
Agriculture is the largest human user of freshwater, accounting for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals (FAO), though the exact figure is uncertain and should be treated as an approximation.

The food system accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of global anthropogenic GHG emissions: IPCC SRCCL (2019) estimated 21–37% (medium confidence); Crippa et al. (2021, EDGAR-FOOD) estimated about 34% for 2015 (~18 Gt CO2e); Poore & Nemecek (2018) estimated about 26% for food production.

The USDA/NRCS organizes soil-health management around four principles — minimize soil disturbance, keep the soil covered, maximize living roots, maximize biodiversity — implemented via no-till/reduced-till, cover crops, crop rotation, IPM, and agroforestry.

USDA and EPA estimate that 30–40% of the U.S. food supply goes uneaten; a 2014 USDA ERS study estimated retail- and consumer-level food loss at 31% of the supply in 2010 (~133 billion pounds, ~$161 billion).
In 2015 the USDA and EPA set the first U.S. national goal to cut food loss and waste in half by 2030 against a 2016 baseline.

Transport ('food miles') is only about 6% of food-system emissions globally, so what a food is matters far more for its carbon footprint than how far it traveled; beef emits roughly 25 kg CO2e per 100 g protein versus under 1 kg for peas/lentils.
Shifting toward plant-rich diets is evidence-based as a way to lower food's footprint, but individual dietary choices also reflect culture, health, budget, and personal values.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The precise share of global GHG emissions attributable to the food system.
positions: IPCC SRCCL (2019): 21–37% of net anthropogenic emissions, including pre- and post-production (medium confidence).
Crippa et al. (2021, Nature Food/EDGAR-FOOD): about 34% of the global total in 2015 (~18 Gt CO2e).
Poore & Nemecek (2018, Science): about 26% for food production.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Differences stem from system boundaries (what stages are counted) and base year. The lesson presents 'roughly a quarter to a third' and attributes any specific figure to its dated source rather than asserting one exact number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The reliability of the widely cited '70% of freshwater withdrawals' figure for agriculture.
positions: FAO and standard references cite ~70% (recent AQUASTAT ~72%).
A 2024 analysis (PMC) found much of the supporting citation chain lacks empirical grounding and the true share could span a wide range.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states ~70% as an approximation and flags the uncertainty, while noting agriculture is unambiguously the dominant water-using sector.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced claims about food systems; none of it was usable as evidence.
Draft vocabulary defined the topic circularly ('A foundational Environmental Sustainability concept covered in this lesson') and defined only generic study-skills terms.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all placeholder boilerplate with sourced substance on land, water, emissions, practices, waste, and diet.
Added dated, attributed emissions figures with an explicit range instead of an undated single number.
Added the food-miles misconception correction, which the draft lacked entirely.
Rewrote vocabulary to be non-circular and independently defined.

sourceRecords.title: Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Landmark 2018 meta-analysis of ~38,700 farms across 119 countries and 570 LCA studies. Supports: food production ~26% of global GHG emissions; beef ~25 kg CO2e per 100 g protein vs <1 kg for peas/lentils; transport a small share of footprint; plant-based diets can cut food emissions substantially. Cited from DOI 10.1126/science.aaq0216 and the Oxford ORA copy; figures cross-checked via Our World in Data.

sourceRecords.title: Food systems are responsible for a third of global anthropogenic GHG emissions (EDGAR-FOOD)
sourceRecords.provider: Nature Food; Crippa et al. (FAO / EC Joint Research Centre)
sourceRecords.notes: 2021 study introducing the EDGAR-FOOD database. Supports: food-system emissions ~34% of the global total in 2015, ~18 Gt CO2e; share declined from 44% (1990) to 34% (2015) even as absolute emissions rose. Confirmed via the FAO newsroom summary of the same study.

sourceRecords.title: IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land (SRCCL), Chapter 5: Food Security
sourceRecords.notes: 2019 report. Supports: food systems account for 21–37% of total net anthropogenic GHG emissions including pre- and post-production (medium confidence); within-farm-gate crop/livestock 9–14%, land use/land-use change 5–14%, supply chain 5–10%. Used to anchor the emissions range.

sourceRecords.title: Food systems account for more than one third of global greenhouse gas emissions
sourceRecords.notes: FAO newsroom summary of the EDGAR-FOOD / Crippa et al. 2021 result: ~34% of global anthropogenic GHG in 2015, ~18 Gt CO2e; methane ~35% of food-system GHG. Corroborates the peer-reviewed source.

sourceRecords.title: Food Loss and Waste / Food Waste FAQs
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: USDA/EPA estimate 30–40% of the U.S. food supply is uneaten; USDA co-leads the 2030 halving goal. U.S. federal work, generally public domain.

sourceRecords.title: United States 2030 Food Loss and Waste Reduction Goal
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: USDA and EPA jointly announced (Sept 16, 2015) the first national goal to cut food loss and waste in half by 2030 against a 2016 baseline (328 to 164 lbs/person); '30 to 40 percent of the food supply is never eaten.' U.S. federal work.

sourceRecords.title: The Estimated Amount, Value, and Calories of Postharvest Food Losses at the Retail and Consumer Levels in the United States (EIB-121)
sourceRecords.provider: USDA Economic Research Service; Buzby, Wells & Hyman
sourceRecords.notes: 2014 ERS study. Supports: 31% food loss at retail and consumer levels in 2010 (~133 billion pounds, ~$161 billion); meat/poultry/fish the largest share of loss value. U.S. federal work.

sourceRecords.title: Soil Health Principles and Practices
sourceRecords.provider: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) / Farmers.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the four NRCS soil-health principles (minimize disturbance, keep soil covered, maximize living roots, maximize biodiversity) and the practices that implement them: no-till/reduced-till, cover crops, crop rotation, diverse mixes. Cross-checked against the NRCS 'Unlock the Secrets in the Soil' factsheet (2021) and North Dakota NRCS soil-health principle pages.

sourceRecords.title: Environmental Impacts of Food Production
sourceRecords.provider: Our World in Data (Hannah Ritchie & Max Roser)
sourceRecords.notes: CC BY 4.0. Aggregates Poore & Nemecek (2018) and FAO data. Supports: food ~26% of global GHG; half of habitable land farmed (three-quarters for livestock, 18% of calories); ~70% of freshwater withdrawals to agriculture; transport ~6% of food emissions; beef vs peas per-100g-protein figures. Only facts used; no text reproduced.
